round: the reviewer's first round on the new scope: three blocking and four minor, all fixed in one commit; three threads declined as moot, their files no longer on this branch

proof.criterion: Blocking 1 — the deployment's cluster namespace was written out in a shell command in `.legion/INFRA-71/plan.json:100`, on a branch of a public repository, which the architect's standing rule and AGENTS.md's public-repository paragraph both forbid.
proof.surface: The branch's own tracked tree, swept file by file, and the file itself.
proof.command: jj file list | xargs grep -InE for the namespace in a Kubernetes context (`-n <ns>`, `namespace: <ns>`, `namespaces/<ns>`, `<ns> namespace`, `namespace <ns>`) and grep -Il -F for the compute class, the scratch storage class and the admission policy's name ; .github/scripts/check-private-names.sh ; python3 -c json.load on the edited handoff
proof.observed: The field now carries the sentence alone and says in place that it was redacted and why. Across all 4734 tracked files there is no hit for the namespace in any Kubernetes context, and none at all for the compute class, the scratch storage class or the policy name. The handoff still parses as JSON, and the repository's own private-name check passes — which proves nothing here and is recorded as passing for that reason.
proof.negativeControl: The exposure, recorded rather than purged, on the architect's ruling: the literal stood in `.legion/INFRA-71/plan.json:100` from the plan handoff's push (commit 761e24ff, 2026-10-24 05:23Z) until this commit, about two hours, and the blob stays reachable through pull request #2092 because the pushed commit is not rewritten — a force push would cost the reviewer's approval by SHA and the daemon's recorded heads and would not unpublish it. Retro removes `.legion/` from the head that merges, so main never carries it. Nothing in the repository could have caught it: `check-private-names.sh` knows the deployment repository, the company and their hosts, not a namespace, and the tester's own private-name proof greps the five non-handoff paths by construction.

proof.criterion: Blocking 2 — the step that demonstrated reaching the workload ran `psql`, which no role container has, in a section that forbids both ways of getting one.
proof.surface: This role container, running the section's own published check, and the image itself.
proof.command: which psql ; the `python3 - <<'PY'` block extracted verbatim from the published sh block and run against a port that listens and one that does not
proof.observed: `which psql` finds nothing. The published snippet prints `answered` for `kubernetes.default.svc:443` and fails `TimeoutError: timed out` for `kubernetes.default.svc:5432` after its ten seconds — both outcomes a role will meet, and the timeout is also the symptom the missing reachability label produces. The section now says in as many words that the role container has no client for any of these servers, that `exec` into the workload's pod is closed and that installing one in its own pod is the withheld `operator-setup` row, so speaking a server's protocol means a client library onto the issue's own disk, the way every other tool that works from the checkout arrives.
proof.negativeControl: The two routes the section forbids are not quietly reintroduced: nothing in the sequence runs `kubectl exec` or installs into the pod, and the check is a connection rather than a query, which is the most the image can honestly do. A real query would need a client the image does not carry; it is named as the issue's own disk rather than written as an unexecuted command.

proof.criterion: Blocking 3 — nothing told a role to name its workload for its issue, in a namespace every project's agents share under one identity, so two roles following the section collide and the documented delete takes the other's running workload.
proof.surface: The section's text and its manifest, driven against live admission under the issue-scoped name.
proof.command: the manifest extracted from the section with `<workload>` filled as the new paragraph tells a role to fill it, through kubectl apply --dry-run=server
proof.observed: `job.batch/infra-71-postgres created (server dry run)` — the name the section now prescribes is admitted. The paragraph sits before the manifest, names the convention (`<issue key lowercased>-<what it is>`) beside the two issue-scoped names this runbook already uses, and spells out what the obvious name costs: the second apply patches or fails on immutable fields, the wait selects the other role's pod by label, and the delete takes its database and Service away mid-test.
proof.negativeControl: The collision is not hypothetical and is written as the sequence's own outcome rather than as advice: every step that names the workload selects by name or by `job-name` label, neither of which distinguishes two roles' workloads, which is why the name is the only place it can be fixed.

proof.criterion: The four minor findings, taken in the same pass: the gate's `no` branch is not what a credential-less role sees; the promise that every mistake is refused naming its rule is untrue of the reachability label; the manifests carry a password into a public repository's checkout; the last line asks for Services before the grant exists.
proof.surface: The section's text against this cluster and this image, and the reviewer's own measurement of the credential-less case.
proof.command: the section re-read against the measurements: kubectl auth can-i create jobs|services here ; the label bullet against the eight breakages already measured ; the sequence's first line ; kubectl apply of the Service pre-apply
proof.observed: The gate paragraph now says a role with no credential gets neither answer — no kubeconfig and no `KUBECONFIG`, so `kubectl` builds no in-cluster configuration, falls back to `localhost:8080`, prints the connection refusal and the `doesn't have a resource type 'jobs'` warning, and may still exit 0 — and that anything other than a bare `yes` is to be read as not having it. The promise is qualified where it is made, and the label bullet opens by saying this is the one rule admission does not enforce, naming the symptom (the reachability check timing out against a Service that has endpoints) and the check (the pod's own labels against the declaration). The sequence opens `cd "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}"` with its reason, and ends `kubectl get jobs,pods`, with a clause saying the Service steps are refused `Forbidden` before the apply and that the refusal is the deployment's state rather than a fault in the manifest.
proof.negativeControl: The label claim is checked by what the measurements do *not* contain: eight breakages here and nineteen in the tester's round cover every rule in the list and none covers a missing label, because there is no refusal to measure — which is exactly the reviewer's finding, and is why the bullet now carries a symptom instead of a promise.

filesChanged: docs/kubernetes.md: the gate's third answer, the qualified promise, the label bullet with its symptom and check, the naming paragraph, the sequence written outside the checkout, the reachability check in place of `psql` with the paragraph explaining it, and the pre-apply clause on the Service steps.
.legion/INFRA-71/plan.json: the departure's `spec` field redacted to its sentence.
trickyParts: The namespace is a common English word, so sweeping for it needs a Kubernetes context (`-n <ns>`, `namespace: <ns>`, `namespaces/<ns>`, `<ns> namespace`) rather than the bare string, which matches 896 files in a tree this size. The other three declaration names are distinctive and were swept bare.

The only honest demonstration this image can give is that the address answers. That is less than the section promised and more than it could deliver: the client that would run a query is not in the image and may not be installed in the pod, so the section names where a client comes from instead of writing a command nobody can run.
deviations: The three threads from the superseded scope are declined rather than fixed: their files are off this branch. The guard's open finding travels to dispatch://INFRA-199 with its commits, which stay in this branch's history.
openQuestions: Specification acceptance 1, 2, 3 and 4 still wait on a person applying dispatch://INFRA-206; the Service half of the sequence is refused `Forbidden` here and is recorded as refused rather than simulated.

The redacted blob stays reachable through this pull request until retro takes `.legion/` off the merging head. That is the architect's ruling and the controller is told; a rewrite was refused for what it would cost.
discoveredComplexity: A document whose steps are run finds its own defects: the deadline rule last round, and this round the fact that the one tool the demonstration reached for is not in the image the document is written for. Neither was visible by reading.
